Agentsensus: Consensus-Compressed Shared Memory for
Multi-Agent Story-World Simulation

A shared long-term memory that merges agents’ equivalent memories into multi-witness records and self-organizes into a navigable memory graph.

Scenarios 三国演义 (80 ticks, 33 active agents) · Russia–Ukraine (40 ticks, 47 active) · 红楼梦 (10-tick pilot, 34 active) Checkpointing every 20 ticks Model gpt-5-mini
Abstract

Multi-agent story-world simulations give every agent a private memory stream, so the same event is stored once per witness, memories of one plotline are scattered across isolated stores, and nothing connects what one agent knows to what another experienced. We present Agentsensus, a story-world simulation framework whose shared long-term memory performs consensus compression: every deposited memory is atomized into self-contained statements, semantically matched against the store, and — when an LLM judge deems two statements equivalent — merged into a single record whose owner-set is the union of its witnesses. Atomized pieces of one compound memory are automatically linked (affiliated), and recall automatically expands one hop along these links, so the memory self-organizes into a graph that retrieval exploits without any agent-side memory management. On an 80-tick simulation of Romance of the Three Kingdoms seeded with memories sedimented from chapters 1–40, and compared under an equal-granularity protocol against three per-agent memory baselines (Generative-Agents-style streams, G-Memory-style hierarchical graph, ACL-based collaborative memory), consensus is the only backend whose simulation memories become shared (19% multi-owner, merges reaching 6 witnesses; baselines 0%) and linked (97% with affiliated edges; baselines 0%), while also writing the fewest entries (974 vs 1251–1455). The emergent memory graph tracks the story’s social structure: agents who talk overlap in memory 23× more than those who don’t, linked memories share witnesses at Jaccard 0.77 vs 0.04, and cross-agent memory links run almost exclusively between conversing agents. A 40-tick replication on a real-world Russia–Ukraine scenario reproduces the full structural signature — sharing grows 6%→9%→14% as the horizon doubles and redoubles, with one presidential directive merging across ten institutional witnesses — confirming that consensus structure compounds with horizon in a real-world setting.

1 Introduction

Story-world simulation places dozens of LLM-driven characters into a fictional world and lets a narrative unfold from their interactions. The dominant memory design, inherited from Generative Agents [1] and adopted by most subsequent frameworks [2, 8], gives each character a private, append-only memory stream. This is faithful to individual cognition, but for a shared world it creates three structural problems that worsen with scale:

  • P1 — Witness-multiplied redundancy. Every shared experience is stored once per participant: a war council attended by ten officers produces ten near-identical records, and a novel-seeded world multiplies this by thousands of canonical events. Storage, embedding cost, and retrieval-index size all scale with the number of witnesses rather than the number of events — in our testbed the per-agent baselines carry 3× the entries of the consensus store for the same seeded history.
  • P2 — Fragmented, divergence-prone world knowledge. The same event exists as N independently-worded copies that only drift further apart as agents paraphrase, summarize, and reflect. No mechanism reconciles them, no record knows its counterparts exist, and nothing connects a courier’s report to the battle it describes or the order it triggers — the connective tissue of the story exists nowhere in the memory substrate, only implicitly in the transcript. Retrieval consequently returns one agent’s partial, possibly stale view even when the collective already holds the full picture.
  • P3 — Memory management that agents never perform. Stream designs expose maintenance operations — linking related records, revising stale ones, forgetting duplicates — and implicitly rely on agents to use them. Empirically they do not: across two models and all four backends we test, agents issued zero calls to every discretionary memory-management action, even with documentation, worked examples, and an id-free interface (§5.6). A memory architecture that depends on agent-side curation therefore never acquires structure in practice.

Agentsensus answers all three problems with one architectural commitment: the world’s memory is a single shared store, and sharing is computed, not assumed. Memories remain owner-scoped — an agent recalls only what it owns — but when two agents record the same event, an equivalence mechanism detects it and folds the records into one entry owned by both (addressing P1 and the divergence half of P2). Pieces split from one compound memory are automatically cross-linked and recall automatically surfaces linked memories the caller also owns, giving the store the connective tissue P2 demands. And because of P3, every structural mechanism runs inside remember and recall themselves — the only two memory operations agents demonstrably use — rather than being delegated to agent-side curation.

Contributions.

  • A story-world simulation framework with a deterministic tick-barrier scheduler, passive environments and information carriers, kernel-held conversation threads with distance-delayed delivery, and full-system checkpoints enabling bit-for-bit resumption.
  • A consensus-compressed shared memory: self-contained atomization, semantic-prefilter + LLM-judged equivalence merging with owner-set union, automatic affiliation of split pieces, and auto-expanding owner-scoped recall.
  • An equal-granularity, simulation-only evaluation protocol against three faithful baseline reimplementations, isolating the memory mechanism from confounds of storage granularity and seeded content.
  • A three-layer case-study methodology (interaction graph, memory-affiliation graph, ownership relation) quantifying how the emergent memory structure tracks the story’s social structure.

2 Related Work

Memory for LLM agents.

Generative Agents [1] established the stream-of-memories design — per-agent records scored by recency, importance, and relevance, periodically compressed into reflections — which subsequent agent frameworks largely inherit [8]. MemGPT [4] treats context as a memory hierarchy managed by the LLM itself; Reflexion [5] persists self-feedback across episodes. Closer to our graph mechanisms, HippoRAG [6] indexes a corpus as an entity graph for multi-hop retrieval, and A-MEM [7] links an agent’s notes into an evolving network. These systems structure the memory of one agent or one corpus; Agentsensus structures memory across agents, with ownership as a first-class dimension.

Multi-agent memory.

G-Memory [3] organizes a multi-agent system’s history into a hierarchical insight/query/interaction graph queried at both team and agent level. Collaborative-memory designs [9] share fragments across users under dynamic access control. Both keep per-contributor records intact; neither merges equivalent records across contributors — the core of consensus compression — nor derives the memory graph automatically from deposit-time structure.

Story-world simulation.

BookWorld [2] builds interactive agent societies from novels, with per-character memories extracted from the source text; our sedimentation stage follows the same motivation. Agentsensus differs in making the sedimented and runtime memory a single consensus store, and in evaluating the memory substrate itself (footprint, sharing, graph structure) rather than only the produced narrative.

3 The Agentsensus Framework

3.1  Overview

Agentsensus consists of three subsystems (Figure 1): an offline sedimentation pipeline that turns a source novel into a memory-grounded initial world; a deterministic tick-barrier kernel that schedules agents, routes messages, and snapshots the full system; and the consensus shared memory, whose write and read paths embed all of the structural mechanisms of §1. Data flows left to right at start-up (sedimentation seeds the store and the world state) and cycles between kernel and store at run time: Phase-2 action effects write into the store and the conversation threads, and both feed the next tick’s agent views through owner-scoped recall and the conversation roster.

3.2  World model and tick-barrier kernel

Entities. A world is a set of agents on a location map with pairwise travel distances. Characters are LLM-driven: each holds a persona, a goal stack, a status register, and a short-term FIFO of recent actions; each decision is one LLM call that receives a rendered view (tick, goals, status, FIFO, co-located agents, conversation roster, known locations, plus contextual hints) and returns one action as JSON. Environments and information carriers are passive: they own memories (deposited by sedimentation or by characters’ act_on) but never take turns — a character’s act_on/read is served synchronously by the kernel against the target’s own memories, costing no extra LLM calls and giving places and documents durable, queryable state.

Scheduling. Each tick runs two phases under a barrier. Phase 1 builds every awake character’s view from the same pre-tick snapshot and issues all decisions concurrently; because views are frozen before any decision, LLM latency cannot change what any agent observes. Phase 2 applies the returned actions sequentially in a fixed agent order, so conflicting effects resolve deterministically and event order is reproducible independent of API timing. Agents sleep only by explicit wait; a single sleep is capped (20 ticks) after we observed uncapped waits produce narrative deadlocks — a character who delegated a task and slept “until the report arrives” was simply never messaged again and stayed silent for 52 ticks. A wake=true message still interrupts sleep early.

Messaging. Messages are not agent-held inboxes but kernel-held conversation threads, one per interlocutor pair. Co-located speech delivers at the next tick; remote messages travel for their map distance in ticks, so information propagates at the speed of couriers rather than instantaneously. Delivery increments the recipient’s unread counter (surfaced in its view roster) and, by default, wakes it; reading is an explicit read_thread action. The same threads also log observation and environment interactions, giving each pair a complete interaction history.

Checkpointing. Every 20 ticks the kernel atomically snapshots the complete system — each agent’s short-term state (FIFO, goal stack, status, sleep timer), kernel runtime (presence, in-transit moves, undelivered messages, conversation threads, event counter), and the entire memory store including embeddings. A resumed run continues bit-for-bit; all 80-tick results in §5 are four resumed 20-tick stages of one continuous run per backend.

3.3  Sedimentation: from novel to memory-grounded world

The pipeline converts chapters 1–40 into the initial world in four steps. (i) Extraction and attribution: an LLM pass extracts events chapter by chapter and attributes each to the characters who witnessed it, producing atomic, story-ordered records with owner-sets. (ii) Per-backend ingest: each memory backend stores these events under its own rule — the consensus store keeps one merged row per event carrying the full owner-set, while per-agent baselines fan out one row per witness — so every method starts from the initial state its own mechanism would have produced, and baseline machinery (importance scoring, reflection, distillation) is run over the sediment before tick 0. (iii) Boundary-state finalization: each character’s aliveness and location at the story boundary are extracted from its own memory timeline (with a canon-knowledge fallback anchored to the boundary chapter); characters dead by chapter 40 are archived — they keep their memories as owners but are never scheduled — and living ones are placed at their last grounded location. (iv) The result: 191 characters (33 active), ~6,000 consensus events, a world whose knowledge and geography are both grounded in the text.

3.4  The consensus shared memory

Data model. The store is a single vector collection whose rows are (text, embedding, owner-set, affiliated-set, metadata). Owner membership is additionally materialized as indexed per-agent flags, so owner-scoped retrieval is a server-side filter rather than a post-hoc scan; the affiliated-set holds ids of related rows and is what makes the store a graph.

Write path. Every remember(text) runs four stages. (1) Atomization: a compound deposit is split by an LLM into atomic statements, each required to be self-contained — pronouns resolved to names, who/what/where carried over — so a statement is interpretable without its siblings. All four backends share this exact stage (§4.3), making entry counts comparable by construction. (2) Candidate pre-filter: each atom is embedded and matched against the store by cosine kNN with a deliberately permissive threshold (0.70): self-contained phrasings of the same event from different viewpoints embed measurably further apart than near-identical wordings, and at the conventional 0.86 zero cross-witness sim memories ever reached candidacy. (3) Equivalence judging: an LLM judge inspects the candidates and either selects the one that describes the same event or declines. The pre-filter only bounds the judge’s candidate list; the judge is the actual gate, so the permissive threshold trades a few extra judge calls for recall of true matches. (4) Merge or insert: on a match the records fold into one row — owner-sets union, affiliated-sets union, the shorter text is kept — so N witnesses of one event cost one row; otherwise a fresh row is inserted. Finally, auto-affiliation mutually links the atoms split from one deposit: the memory graph is built as a side-effect of writing, by the mechanism rather than the agent.

Read path. recall(query) retrieves the top-k semantic matches among rows the caller owns, then follows each hit’s affiliated edges one hop and appends linked rows the caller also owns, marked via_affiliated. A single recall therefore returns an event’s scattered pieces together — in the 80-tick run every one of the 51 recalls returned expanded context (≈28 linked memories per call). Expansion is deliberately uncapped; its cost is measured in §5.2.

Cost placement. The design pays at write time (one atomization call when a deposit is compound, one judge call when candidates pass the pre-filter) to keep the store small and structured; reads add only vector lookups. §5.2’s latency instrumentation quantifies both sides against the baselines.

3.5  Query-addressed operations and the design rule

No memory operation takes a raw id. forget, revise_memory, and the affiliation operations address a memory by a natural-language query that the kernel resolves to the caller’s best-matching owned row, so owner-scoping is enforced at resolution and there is no id for an agent to mishandle. The design responds to a robust behavioral finding: LLM agents never thread opaque ids across turns — in earlier runs every id-based operation had ≈0 uses. Query addressing removes that interface barrier; the observation that agents still issue zero discretionary memory-management calls (§5.6) is what elevates “structure must live inside remember/recall” from an implementation choice to the framework’s central design rule.

4 Experimental Setup

4.1  Scenarios

三国演义 chapters 1–40 are sedimented onto 191 canonical characters (33 active at the boundary, the rest archived as dead; ~6,000 consensus events). All four backends then run the same 80-tick simulation — same scenario file, same action repertoire, same model (gpt-5-mini; embeddings text-embedding-3-small) — in four checkpointed 20-tick stages.

To test that the mechanisms are not an artifact of one fictional world, the second scenario is real-world: a timeline of the Russia–Ukraine conflict sedimented through 2026-07 (1,533 events over 170 entities). Real-world boundary semantics replace the novel’s: a figure is archived if, by the boundary, they are dead or out of the conflict’s stage (out of office, dismissed, disbanded), with placements grounded in the timeline or, failing that, the person’s workplace/role (final cast: 47 active, 14 archived, manually verified). All four backends run the same 40-tick simulation under the identical fairness protocol.

The third scenario returns to fiction in a different register: 红楼梦 (Dream of the Red Chamber), chapters 1–40 sedimented onto 152 registry characters (6,506 consensus events; chapters 41–80 held out). The active cast is the 37 characters above the memory threshold (34 living; 秦可卿, 贾瑞 and 秦钟, dead by chapter 40, stay archived owners), and the boundary state is a freeze-frame of chapter 40’s garden banquet — 贾母 and 刘姥姥 at 大观楼, the touring party at 蘅芜苑, the musicians at 藕香榭 — grounded per character in the sediment and manually verified. Where 三国 is war and statecraft among factions, 红楼 is dense domestic society — one household, fine-grained relationships — a different social topology for the same mechanisms. All four backends run the same 10-tick pilot under the identical fairness protocol.

4.2  Baselines

  • Generative-Agents memory [1]: per-agent private streams; insert-time importance scoring; reflection synthesis over high-importance windows.
  • G-Memory [3]: shared store organized as interaction/insight tiers with periodic LLM distillation into insight nodes and bi-level retrieval over provenance edges.
  • Collaborative memory [9]: per-owner fragments guarded by access-control lists; recall is ACL-filtered server-side.

All three ingest the sediment under their own rule (one row per witness) and run their own machinery over it (GA importance+reflections; G-Memory distillation) before tick 0, so each starts from a self-consistent initial state.

4.3  Fairness protocol

Equal granularity. Every backend routes remember through the same atomization code with the same self-containment requirement. Entry counts are therefore directly comparable; the only remaining difference is what each mechanism does with identical atoms.

Simulation-only accounting. All reported numbers cover memories the simulation itself generated (remember/act_on deposits). Sedimented content and baseline by-products (GA reflection nodes, G-Memory distillation nodes) are excluded on all sides.

4.4  Metrics

  • Structure (deterministic): sim-entry count; share of multi-owner entries; share of entries with affiliated edges.
  • Continuation quality (LLM-judged, mean±std over 3 scorings of the sim transcript): grounding — the fraction of the sim’s own events consistent with the canon; trajectory — agreement of character arcs with reference arcs extracted from each world’s held-out continuation (三国: chapters 41–60; Russia–Ukraine: the timeline beyond the 2024-04 boundary); narrative — judged coherence/drama/fidelity (1–5); goal pursuit — whether each agent’s actions consistently pursue its declared goals (judged against the goal stack the agent itself maintains; defined here, measurement deferred — achievement itself is deliberately not scored, since a faithful tragedy requires goals to fail). The verbose Russia–Ukraine transcripts are compacted to the judge’s context window (messages truncated to 280 chars, lines sampled evenly when needed); 三国 fits untruncated.
  • Operation latency (§5.2): per-call wall-clock time of remember/recall, timed in the kernel around the backend call so each mechanism’s internal cost (equivalence judging, importance scoring, auto-expansion) falls inside the window. Ticks 61–80 are instrumented live; ticks 1–60 are measured by replaying each stage’s logged operations against the store state the stage started from (checkpoint-exact for stages 2–3; the first stage’s GA/G-Memory replay stores lack prime by-products, ≈3–5% of rows).
  • Three-layer alignment (§5.4): relations between the interaction graph, the affiliation graph, and the ownership relation.

5 Results

5.1  Footprint and structure

At equal granularity, consensus writes the fewest sim memories in both long-horizon worlds (三国: 974 vs 1251–1455; Russia–Ukraine: 814 vs 1091–1268) because merging folds witnesses together; in the 10-tick 红楼 pilot the spread (62–98 entries) is still within run-to-run variance and no backend separates. What separates from the first tick is structure: in every world consensus is the only backend whose memories become shared and linked (19%/97% in 三国, 14%/99% in Russia–Ukraine, 13%/87% in 红楼), against 0% for every baseline.

5.1.1  三国演义

Discussion. Two readings matter here. First, the footprint gap is mechanistic, not behavioral: all four backends receive the same actions and atomize identically, so the 481-entry spread between consensus and the largest baseline is exactly the number of times the equivalence judge folded one agent’s record into another’s — each fold is a deduplicated witness (P1). Second, the structural columns are all-or-nothing by design: per-agent stores have no cross-agent rows to merge and no deposit-siblings to link, so the 19% / 97% columns measure capabilities the baselines lack architecturally, not parameters they tuned differently.

Merged records are precisely the cross-viewpoint deduplication the mechanism targets — 38 memories carry three or more witnesses (maximum 6):

owners = [hanxiandi, xiahoudun, xiahouyuan, xushu, yuejin, yujin]  “夏侯渊率三百轻骑分三路从许昌出城侦察。”
owners = [hanxiandi, xiahoudun, xushu, yujin, zhangliao]  “乐进督管许昌的粮草与军需。”
owners = [hanxiandi, xiahoudun, xushu, yuejin, yujin]  “张辽被任为许昌防务的总摄指挥。”

5.1.2  Russia–Ukraine

Discussion. The same two readings hold at one eighth the horizon: the 19–30% footprint gap is again exactly the number of equivalence-judge folds, and the structural columns remain all-or-nothing — 0% for every per-agent baseline. What is new is the real-world flavor of the folds: equivalence merges a person’s record into their institution’s — the same mechanism that fuses two officers’ views of one battle fuses a spokesperson’s statement with its organization’s record of it.

Merged records again pair one event seen from two sides — characteristically a person and their institution:

owners = [guterres, un]  “António Guterres at UN Headquarters in New York asked the United Nations to assemble a mediation team comprising DPA, OCHA, WFP, UN Political Affairs, and UN Legal to support renewal of the Black Sea grain agreement.”
owners = [podolyak, ukrainian_government]  “Mykhailo Podolyak reported that overnight Russian drone strikes struck Dnipropetrovsk Oblast.”
owners = [kremlin, sobyanin]  “Moscow Mayor Sergey Sobyanin requested authorization to release public instructions to Moscow residents.”

5.1.3  红楼梦

Discussion. The pilot separates the two claims of §5.1 cleanly. The structural claim reproduces in full at ten ticks: 13% shared (10 multi-owner entries, 3 with three witnesses), 87% linked, 0% on both columns for every baseline — the household setting merges exactly as the battlefield and the war room did, folding 王熙凤’s seating instructions into the records of the kinsmen who received them. The footprint claim does not yet: at 62–98 entries the four backends are within noise of one another and consensus (77) is not the smallest. This is the expected small-sample regime — with ~8 memory-worthy events per tick, ten folds cannot outweigh ordinary variance in what agents choose to remember; 三国’s own early ticks showed the same interleaving before deduplication compounded. The 40-tick extension will test whether the footprint gap opens on the horizon curve as it did in both other worlds.

Merged records in the household world fold family witnesses of one scene:

owners = [jiazhen, liulaolao, wangxifeng]  “王熙凤交代薛宝钗与薛姨妈在旁协助伺候贾母。”
owners = [jiarong, jiazhen, wangxifeng]  “王熙凤在大观楼要求贾蓉和贾珍将座位按长幼顺序摆放。”
owners = [jiahuan, jiazheng, mingyan]  “贾政在贾府下令召贾宝玉到贾政书房读书守礼。”

5.2  Growth and operation latency

The footprint gap of Table 1 accumulates tick by tick, and its price is paid at write time. We show both sides for each scenario.

5.2.1  三国演义

Discussion. The system-level curves separate almost from the start and diverge steadily — the merge saves entries at a roughly constant rate, so its absolute savings compound with horizon rather than saturating; there is no sign of the gap closing by tick 80. The per-agent curves show the same mechanism from the individual’s side: growth is stair-stepped (a burst when a character is at the center of a plotline, plateaus when off-stage), and the ranking tracks narrative centrality rather than raw talkativeness — 徐庶 leads because the 徐庶-recruitment arc dominates the middle game, and every merge credits a shared event to all of its witnesses’ curves at once.

Discussion. The two panels show where each design pays. Writes are LLM-bound: every backend pays the shared atomization call, on top of which Generative-Agents adds a per-atom importance call (the most expensive line, 35–75s) and consensus adds the equivalence judge (26–57s), while G-Memory and collaborative write for 10–25s with no per-deposit reasoning beyond atomization. Reads are vector-bound and cheap everywhere (≤1.4s), and — notably — consensus recall is the cheapest of the four (≈0.35s) despite returning ≈28 additional linked memories per call: auto-expansion is plain row lookup, whereas G-Memory’s bi-level retrieval pays for graph traversal with extra vector queries (0.7–1.1s). Neither panel trends upward over 80 ticks: at this scale, store growth (≈7k–22k rows) does not yet move per-call latency, so the consensus premium is a roughly constant per-write tax — the price of P1’s deduplication — paid where agents are least latency-sensitive.

5.2.2  Russia–Ukraine

Discussion. Both figures replay the 三国 dynamics at a shorter horizon. The system curves separate from tick ~3 with consensus lowest and the gap widening, and per-agent growth again concentrates on the situation’s protagonists. The latency ordering of Figure 6 reproduces: writes are LLM-bound (Generative-Agents’ per-atom importance calls most expensive, consensus paying the equivalence-judge tax), while reads are vector-bound and sub-second for all four backends, with consensus recall cheapest despite auto-expansion.

5.2.3  红楼梦

Discussion. The domestic world writes more slowly than either other scenario (~8 entries/tick systemwide vs ~20 in Russia–Ukraine) — garden conversation generates fewer memory-worthy events than a war — and the growth curves interleave rather than separate at this horizon, consistent with the footprint reading of Figure 4. Per-agent growth still concentrates on the situation’s protagonists: the banquet’s hosts and guests (贾珍, 元春, 李纨, 刘姥姥, 王熙凤) own the fastest-growing stores. Write latency is LLM-bound and noisy in 2-tick bins at this call volume, with consensus’s equivalence-judge tax visible mid-run; the read side reproduces both other worlds exactly — consensus recall is cheapest (≈0.33s) despite auto-expansion returning ≈39 linked memories per call, and G-Memory’s bi-level retrieval is dearest (0.7–1.5s).

5.3  Continuation quality

Compression does not cost judged quality in either world. In 三国, consensus scores highest on narrative and is competitive elsewhere; in Russia–Ukraine all four backends land within overlapping error bars on every metric, with consensus tied-best on grounding and trajectory. The structural gaps of §5.1 do not translate into behavioral penalties.

5.3.1  三国演义

Discussion. The quality profile is consistent with what compression should and should not affect. Narrative coherence benefits from consensus (4.25, the clear leader): agents recalling one shared record of an event act on consistent premises, where baseline agents can act on N drifting paraphrases of it. Trajectory sits in the pack (0.68 vs 0.59–0.72): arc-following depends mostly on the persona and goal machinery all backends share. Grounding is mid-pack (0.86 vs 0.83–0.92, overlapping error bars): merging keeps the shorter of two equivalent texts, which occasionally discards a viewpoint detail a canon-consistency judge rewards. None of the differences approach the structural gaps of Figure 2 — the mechanisms separate on architecture, not on judged behavior.

5.3.2  Russia–Ukraine

Discussion. The real-world replication is a wash — which is the point. Grounding is uniformly high (0.95–0.96: institutional actors reciting real capabilities rarely fabricate), trajectory is tied within error bars (0.87 for consensus vs 0.83–0.86), and narrative spreads 3.67–4.08 with overlapping whiskers and no stable leader across scorings. As in 三国, the mechanisms separate on architecture (Figure 3), not on judged behavior: consensus deduplicates 814 entries against the baselines’ 1091–1268 and builds all the structure — while giving none of it back in quality.

5.3.3  红楼梦

Not scored: the 红楼 run is a 10-tick pilot, below the horizon at which grounding, trajectory, and narrative judgments are meaningful (both scored worlds use 40 ticks). Quality scoring follows once the run is extended to a comparable horizon.

5.4  Case study: three graphs over each world

Each world’s consensus run induces the same three graphs: the interaction graph (who talks to whom), the affiliation graph (which memories are linked), and the ownership relation (who owns which memories). For each scenario we show the three layers, then all three in one view, then quantify their pairwise alignment.

5.4.1  三国演义

The three layers — interactive: drag to pan, scroll to zoom, hover for details, drag nodes to rearrange
All three layers in one view
Pairwise alignment of the layers

A↔O Agents who talk own overlapping memories (0.066 vs 0.003, 23×)

Owned-memory-set Jaccard between agent pairs: the 51 talking pairs average 0.066; the 984 non-talking pairs average 0.003. The entire upper tail belongs to talking pairs.

M↔O Linked memories have the same witnesses (0.77 vs 0.04)

Owner-set Jaccard between memory pairs: the 5640 affiliated pairs mass near 1.0 (mean 0.77); unlinked pairs mass at zero (mean 0.04). One event’s pieces belong to one event’s witnesses.

A↔M Cross-agent memory links follow conversations (116.7 vs 0.07 edges)

Affiliated edges running between two agents’ memory sets: talking pairs average 116.7; non-talking pairs 0.07. The memory graph bridges exactly the agents the conversation graph connects.

Synthesis. The three alignments are not three separate facts but one: the consensus mechanisms transcribe the story’s social structure into the memory substrate. Conversations are where shared experience happens, so merges (ownership overlap) land on talking pairs; deposits narrate the conversation an agent just had, so affiliation clusters coincide with events and their witnesses; and cross-agent links therefore run along conversation edges. In a per-agent store all three relations are identically zero — the substrate cannot express them — which is why the case study is run on the consensus backend alone.

A↔O Agents who talk own overlapping memories (0.097 vs 0.0029, 33×)

Talking pairs overlap in memory at 0.097 against 0.0029 for silent pairs — the household’s conversation network and its memory network coincide from the first ten ticks.

M↔O Linked memories have the same witnesses (0.79 vs 0.01)

Affiliated pairs share owners at Jaccard 0.79 against 0.01 for random pairs — the same order-of-magnitude alignment as both other worlds.

A↔M Cross-agent memory links follow conversations (2.09 vs 0.149 edges)

Talking pairs average 2.09 affiliated edges between their memory sets against 0.149 for non-talking pairs — a weaker but present separation at pilot scale.

5.5  Structure compounds with horizon

Shared and linked structure is not a transient: across the 20/40/60-tick checkpoints, sim memories grow roughly linearly while shared memories and affiliated edges grow with them — the merge finds more cross-witness events as the story densifies.

5.5.1  三国演义

5.5.2  Russia–Ukraine

Forty ticks in a second, structurally different world (real entities, institutional actors, English-language events, a live timeline rather than a novel) reproduce every qualitative claim of §5: fewest entries, exclusive sharing and linking, the three-layer alignment, and the latency profile. The horizon effect predicted by 三国 is directly observable here: the sharing rate rose 6%→9%→14% at ticks 10/20/40, three-plus-witness merges went from zero to 23, and the deepest merge grew from two witnesses to 10 — a presidential air-defense directive whose single record is co-owned by the president, his chief of staff and adviser, the interior minister, the air-force and intelligence commanders, and the security service — tracking 三国’s 19% at 80 ticks on the same compounding curve.

5.6  Agents do not manage memory — mechanisms must

Across all four backends and both models tested, agents issued zero calls to every discretionary memory-management action — linking (add/set/remove_affiliated), explicit link-reading (get_affiliated), forgetting, and revision — despite documentation, worked skill examples, and the id-free query interface. In contrast, the two mechanism-embedded operations carried everything: remember (with atomization, merging, auto-affiliation inside) and recall (with auto-expansion inside; 51/51 recalls returned linked context). We take this as a design principle for agent memory systems: structure must be a side-effect of the operations agents already perform, not a task delegated to them.

6 Discussion and Limitations

What consensus buys. Under equal granularity and sim-only accounting, consensus dominates structurally — fewest entries, all sharing, all graph structure — and this no longer trades against judged quality (best narrative, competitive elsewhere). The three-layer alignment argues the structure is meaningful: it recovers the story’s social organization from the memory substrate alone.

Limitations. (i) Quality metrics are LLM-judged and noisy; we report 3-scoring means with std, but ranking claims beyond narrative should be treated cautiously. (ii) Results cover one scenario (三国) and one 60-tick horizon; the protocol ports directly to other sedimented worlds and longer runs (checkpoints exist), but those runs remain future work. (iii) Auto-expansion is deliberately uncapped, appending ≈28 linked memories per recall; this enriches context but grows prompts, and its cost–benefit curve is unmeasured. (iv) The equivalence judge and atomizer consume extra LLM calls per deposit — the price of compression is paid at write time. (v) One baseline artifact: G-Memory re-runs distillation on resume (its distill bookkeeping is not check-pointed); sim-only accounting excludes distillation nodes, so reported numbers are unaffected.

7 Conclusion

Agentsensus treats a story world’s memory as a single consensus store: equivalent memories merge across witnesses, split memories link into a graph, and recall walks that graph automatically. On a novel-seeded 80-tick simulation, this yields the smallest memory footprint at equal granularity, the only shared and linked memory structure among four backends, and an emergent memory graph that mirrors the story’s social structure — at no cost to judged narrative quality. The broader lesson is that memory structure in multi-agent systems must be mechanized, not delegated: agents reliably use only remember and recall, so that is where the structure has to live.
